objection: Could the Bible have been changed to make Jesus divine?
answer:
Take a breath — this is one of the most common things people hear today, and it's worth taking seriously rather than just brushing aside. Here's the good news: the "later invention" story doesn't actually match the evidence. Manuscript-wise, we have extraordinary material reaching back astonishingly close to the events themselves — the Rylands fragment of John's Gospel (P52) dates to about AD 125, and P66 and P75 (c. 200) already contain "the Word was God" (John 1:1), "only-begotten God" (John 1:18), and Thomas' "My Lord and my God" (John 20:28) — all more than a century before Nicaea. Nicaea in 325 wasn't a vote to invent Christ's deity; it defended a confession already ancient, one embedded in material older than Paul's own letters.

Scholars who've studied this closely — even ones with no confessional stake in the outcome, like Larry Hurtado and Richard Bauckham — have documented that worship of Jesus as divine erupted among Jewish monotheists within the very first years after the resurrection, not generations later after Greek philosophical corruption. That's remarkable, because Jews were fiercely resistant to worshipping anyone but the one God; this wasn't a gradual drift, it was an explosion at the beginning.

On the copying question: yes, be honest that a handful of verses have real textual variants (1 Timothy 3:16, Acts 20:28 are examples), but even there, on every viable reading the deity of Christ survives — the variants shift a word, not the doctrine. With over 5,800 Greek manuscripts, the New Testament is far and away the best-attested text from the ancient world, and John's testimony to Christ's deity is actually stronger, not weaker, in the earliest copies we have (John 1:18).

So the Jesus you're trusting in — Lord and God, confessed by Thomas himself in the room with him — is the Jesus of the earliest documents and the earliest worship, not a later theological upgrade. Your nervousness is understandable given what you've heard, but the ground under your feet here is firmer than the popular myth suggests.
